steps.label: Rationalise both lines
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two conjugates are needed, one for each line. The factor (a − x) appearing above and below is the check that the working is right.
lines: Take a > 0, so that every square root is defined for x near a.
At x = a the numerator is √(3a) − √(3a) = 0 and the denominator is √(4a) − 2√a = 0, so the form is 0/0.
Multiply above and below by (√(a + 2x) + √(3x)) and by (√(3a + x) + 2√x):

recall.must_convey: That both the numerator and the denominator are rationalised, giving the factors (a − x) and 3(a − x).

steps.why: Both lines are 0 at x = a, so nothing can be read by substitution. Each difference of square roots is removed by its own conjugate, and the same factor (a − x) then appears above and below, ready to cancel.
common_mistakes: Rationalising only the numerator, which leaves 0 in the denominator.
Writing (√(3a + x))² − (2√x)² as (3a + x) − 2x; the 2 must be squared as well.
steps.memory_tip: One conjugate for each difference of roots: the top needs its own and so does the bottom.

steps.label: Cancel (a − x) and put x = a
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Box 2√3/9. The √a cancels, so the answer is the same pure number for every a > 0.
lines: So the expression = [(a − x)(√(3a + x) + 2√x)] / [3(a − x)(√(a + 2x) + √(3x))]

recall.must_convey: That (a − x) cancels, and substituting x = a gives 4√a/(6√(3a)) = 2√3/9.

steps.why: Cancelling (a − x) is allowed because x ≠ a throughout the limit process. After the cancellation the expression is continuous at x = a, so its value there is the limit.
common_mistakes: Cancelling (a − x) against 3(a − x) and writing 3 instead of 1/3.
steps.memory_tip: After both conjugates the value is 4√a over 6√(3a): the √a cancels and 2 over 3√3 is left.
